clue.text: A historic offer to edit film about race

indicators.note: the letters are there to be edited into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: A museum makes a one-off offer and asks someone to edit it.
explanation.walkthrough: Every one of the fourteen letters is used; the whole phrase before 'to edit' is fodder. The film is the 1981 story of runners at the 1924 Olympics.
explanation.definitionFit: Chariots of Fire is a film about Olympic sprinters, so it is literally a film about a race.

clue.text: Have to sleep outside bedroom, it may appear, a disastrous comedown

blocks.note: to crash = to sleep wherever you can
the landing is the space just outside an upstairs bedroom

explanation.surface: A guest reduced to sleeping on the landing outside the bedroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It may appear' flags that LANDING is only one example of what lies outside a bedroom. Read together, crashing on the landing is the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash landing is an aircraft coming down disastrously.

clue.text: Light warning room has no central heating

indicators.note: the room is left without the letters named

blocks.note: a chamber is a room
CH is the standard abbreviation for central heating, taken away

explanation.surface: A notice warning that a room has no heating.
explanation.walkthrough: CH for central heating comes from British estate-agent listings. 'Light warning' is the definition: the amber traffic light warns that red is coming.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is the traffic light that warns drivers to stop.

clue.text: Fool, I sound hesitant to wear skirt when getting up

indicators.note: the skirt is worn around the hesitation
in a down clue, getting up means reading from the bottom

blocks.note: I as written
a sarong is a wrap skirt
um is a hesitant noise, placed after the S of SARONG

explanation.surface: Someone stammering nervously while putting on a skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'getting up' reverses only the part it follows, so the I stays unreversed at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an ignoramus is someone who knows nothing, which is the everyday sense of fool.

clue.text: One extending journeys round continental Europe in the first instance

indicators.note: the journeys go around the other letters
take only the first letter of each word

blocks.note: trips = journeys
first letters of the two words, placed inside TRI…PS

explanation.surface: Someone lengthening trips around mainland Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One extending' looks like a traveller stretching out a tour; it is a muscle, which extends the arm.
explanation.definitionFit: The triceps is the muscle that extends (straightens) the elbow.

clue.text: Still up in Ohio canal? Head back

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom
the reversed word goes inside the canal

blocks.note: O is the postal-style abbreviation for Ohio
a cut is an artificial waterway, a canal
a still is a photograph, a pic; reversed to CIP inside CUT

explanation.surface: A question about whether something is still moored on an Ohio canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' reads as an adverb, but it is the noun: a still photo. 'Cut' for a canal is a British usage for the man-made waterways.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomy term: the occiput is the rear part of the skull, so 'head back' read as a noun phrase.

clue.text: Analyst runs into protracted quarrel

indicators.note: the runs go into the quarrel

blocks.note: a feud is a long-running quarrel
R = runs, the cricket scoring abbreviation

explanation.surface: A psychoanalyst drawn into a long-running dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: R for runs comes from cricket scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis, the archetypal analyst.

clue.text: Students suggested national flag design

indicators.note: the answer is only suggested by the sound of the students' description

blocks.note: students are young sons on the rise

explanation.surface: Students propose a design for their country's flag.
explanation.walkthrough: Students are the up-and-coming generation, rising sons, and SONS sounds like SUN. The flag is Japan's.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Japan's flag shows a red sun, and its naval ensign the sun with rays, both called the Rising Sun.

clue.text: Vestment taken by a new saint

indicators.note: the vestment is followed by the next pieces

blocks.note: an alb is a white priestly vestment
as written
N = new

explanation.surface: A newly canonised saint receives vestments.
explanation.walkthrough: St Alban is venerated as Britain's first Christian martyr, which is the saint the solver needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Alban is the saint of St Albans, Britain's first martyr.

clue.text: As precaution, banking extremely rare profit

indicators.note: the precaution banks, i.e. holds, the letters inside it
take the extreme letters of rare

blocks.note: in case = as a precaution
first and last letters of rare, inside IN C…ASE

explanation.surface: A cautious investor banking a rare profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banking' is read as saving money; here it means holding the letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the financial sense: an increase in value is a gain, a profit.

clue.text: Husband to Anne Sanders, novel author (not Christian)

indicators.note: novel = new, so the letters take a new form

blocks.note: H = husband
anagram fodder with the H added 'to' it

explanation.surface: A husband married to one Anne Sanders, apparently a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, fitting 'author'; it is the anagram signal. '(not Christian)' tells you to drop the middle name from Hans Christian Andersen.
explanation.definitionFit: Hans Christian Andersen wrote fairy tales; without 'Christian' he is Hans Andersen.

clue.text: Pregnant fish has this laborious progress through water, we hear

indicators.note: the answer sounds like the wordplay phrase

blocks.note: a hard row is laborious rowing through water

explanation.surface: A heavily pregnant fish struggling to swim.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard roe is the eggs of a female fish, as against soft roe, the male's milt.
explanation.definitionFit: A female fish carrying eggs has hard roe.

clue.text: Naughty bits of dessert to finish at end of tea

indicators.note: take the last letter of tea

blocks.note: pud is British slang for pudding, i.e. dessert
to end = to finish
last letter of tea

explanation.surface: Scraps of pudding left over to finish at the end of teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bits of dessert' reads as crumbs; the break falls after 'bits'. In Britain 'pud' is everyday slang for the pudding course.
explanation.definitionFit: Pudenda are the external genitals, coyly 'naughty bits'.

clue.text: Gather in numbers for cycling, then drink

indicators.note: the word is cycled: letters move from front to back

blocks.note: to amass is to gather in quantity; move AM from the front to the back

explanation.surface: Cyclists gathering in numbers and then going for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Cycling AMASS moves its first two letters to the end, giving ASSAM. Assam is a strong black tea from north-east India.
explanation.definitionFit: Assam is a kind of tea, which is a drink.

clue.text: Congenial, so admitting I love my country, suppressing riot

indicators.note: SO lets the phrase inside it
RIOT is held down, i.e. removed

blocks.note: as written, wrapped round the rest
I'm patriotic = I love my country
removed from IMPATRIOTIC, leaving IMPATIC inside S…O

explanation.surface: A friendly patriot keeps a lid on the rioting.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase 'I love my country' becomes I'M PATRIOTIC before RIOT is lifted out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A loanword from Italian and Spanish, used in English for someone easy to get along with.

clue.text: Pokes fun, having posed by van Gogh painting

indicators.note: one piece sits beside the next

blocks.note: sat = posed for a portrait
Irises is a van Gogh painting

explanation.surface: Someone mocked for having sat for a van Gogh.
explanation.walkthrough: Irises (1889) is one of van Gogh's best-known canvases.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to satirise someone is to ridicule them, to poke fun.

clue.text: Concept album from Gibraltar?

blocks.note: surface: a themed record; setter: an opera-like album telling one story
surface: a place of origin; setter: Gibraltar is nicknamed the Rock

explanation.surface: A themed record made by a Gibraltarian band.
explanation.walkthrough: Gibraltar is known as the Rock, so an opera from Gibraltar would be a Rock opera; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock opera is a concept album telling one story, such as Tommy.

clue.text: Swear non-stop: question in pub is ridiculous non-event

indicators.note: without its final stop, i.e. last letter
the question goes in with the other letters
the letters are made ridiculous, i.e. jumbled

blocks.note: damn = swear; 'non-stop' then cuts its last letter, leaving DAM
Q = question
as written
as written; Q, PUB and IS are jumbled together

explanation.surface: Someone cursing at a pub quiz that turned out a flop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the verb of the sentence but is fodder, and Q is the standard abbreviation for question.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a squib is a small firework, and a damp one fizzles without a bang, hence a let-down or non-event.

clue.text: Middle Easterner gets a new leader, one who is out of this world

definitions.text: one who is out of this world

indicators.note: the first letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: someone from Iran; its I is replaced by U

explanation.surface: A Middle Eastern figure gets a new, rather otherworldly, leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not name the new first letter; the definition and the checking letters settle it as U.
explanation.definitionFit: A Uranian is an imagined inhabitant of Uranus, so literally from out of this world.

clue.text: Pig slaughtered once in pub

indicators.note: the word is butchered, i.e. jumbled
the jumbled letters go inside the pub

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
ONCE jumbled, placed inside BA…R

explanation.surface: A pig once slaughtered in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' reads as 'formerly' but is the fodder. The grim surface suits the answer: a baconer is a pig raised for bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: A farming term: a baconer is a pig reared to the weight for bacon, so a specific kind of pig.

clue.text: In author’s works, chapter is not by her?

blocks.note: C = chapter
a piece not by the author is anonymous: anon

explanation.surface: A doubt whether a chapter in a writer's collected works is really hers.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'not by her' only hints at anonymity.
explanation.definitionFit: An author's canon is the body of works accepted as genuinely theirs.

clue.text: Across Aegean regularly terrible rain falls

indicators.note: the jumbled rain lies across the Aegean letters
regularly means at regular intervals, so read every other letter of Aegean
terrible rain is in a terrible state, knocked out of its proper order

blocks.note: RAIN jumbled
1st, 3rd and 5th letters of Aegean, inside NI…RA

explanation.surface: A report of dreadful downpours across the Aegean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls' looks like a verb for the rain; it is the noun, naming the waterfall.
explanation.definitionFit: Niagara is the great waterfall on the US–Canada border, the Falls.

clue.text: Maxim: one not the first that’s empty?

indicators.note: the first letter is dropped
what remains has an empty O put in it

blocks.note: 'one' is the maxim itself: MAXIM without its first letter
O = zero, nothing, inserted before the M

explanation.surface: A proverb that begins in the wrong place and is empty?
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' points back to the word MAXIM, so the definition is also worked on. The question mark admits the double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: An axiom is a self-evident truth, a maxim.

clue.text: Bar is excellent but cold inside

indicators.note: but here means with, joining the two pieces
inside says the cold is found within the excellent word

blocks.note: choice = of fine quality
C = cold, as on a tap; placed inside CHO…ICE

explanation.surface: A bar that's great apart from being chilly indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' sounds like a pub, set up by the surface; it is an ice-cream bar. A choc-ice is a British block of ice cream coated in chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: A choc-ice is a chocolate-coated ice-cream bar.

clue.text: One short film about castle finally covered in greenery

indicators.note: a short film is a shortened word for film, so video cut down to vid
the film goes around the letter
take the last letter of castle

blocks.note: I = one
vid is short for video
last letter of castle, inside VI…D

explanation.surface: A short film about a castle smothered in ivy.
explanation.walkthrough: Castle walls covered in ivy is exactly the picture, though castle gives only its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivied means overgrown with ivy, covered in greenery.

clue.text: Islander wrong to coat eyelashes

indicators.note: the wrong goes around the lashes like a coating

blocks.note: a sin is a wrong
cilia are eyelashes; placed inside SI…N

explanation.surface: An islander who applies mascara the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat eyelashes' sets up mascara; coat is the container signal. Cilia is the anatomical word for lashes.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sicilian lives on the island of Sicily.

clue.text: Spice up the Iliad, etc

indicators.note: the letters are stirred up

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

explanation.surface: An invitation to liven up Homer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spice up' reads as one verb; 'up' is the anagram signal and 'etc' makes the definition plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the Iliad is Homer's epic poem, and 'etc' widens it to the class, plural.

clue.text: Choice of grassy areas, nothing special

blocks.note: a common is a public grassy area
or offers a choice between the two
a garden is another grassy area

explanation.surface: Picking between two lawns, neither of them remarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grassy areas' does double duty: one grassy area gives COMMON and the other GARDEN. A common is public open land in a British village or town.
explanation.definitionFit: A British idiom: common-or-garden means ordinary, like the plain species of a plant found everywhere.
